slides.heading: Number Of Ways To Traverse Graph
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Dynamic Programming
slides.narration: Let's solve Number Of Ways To Traverse Graph, a medium dynamic programming problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Paths from top-left to bottom-right of a width x height grid moving only right/down.
Equals C(w+h-2, w-1), computed incrementally to avoid overflow.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Paths from top-left to bottom-right of a width x height grid moving only right or down. Equals C(w plus h-2, w-1), computed incrementally to avoid overflow.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Paths to a cell come from above or from the left; this is also a binomial coefficient.
slides.narration: Paths to a cell come from above or from the left; this is also a binomial coefficient.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
slides.narration: Plain recursion recomputes paths exponentially. A DP grid fills in w times h. Since every path is just an ordering of rights and downs, a binomial coefficient gives the answer directly.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. First row and column have one way
2. Each cell sums its top and left neighbours
slides.narration: Step by step. First, first row and column have one way. Second, each cell sums its top and left neighbours. Third, return the bottom-right cell.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Edges: exactly one way (straight line)
slides.narration: Cells on the top row or left column can only be reached one way.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Each cell = above + left
slides.narration: Every other cell adds the ways from above and from the left. Cell one-one is one plus one, two.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Bottom-right = 10
slides.narration: Filling the grid, the bottom-right cell holds 10 paths.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Shortcut: a binomial coefficient
slides.narration: The solution here uses a shortcut: every path is some arrangement of three rights and two downs, so the count is five choose two, ten. That's constant space and linear time.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We compute n as total moves and k as the smaller dimension minus one, then build the binomial coefficient incrementally: multiply by n minus k plus i and divide by i, which always stays an integer.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of min(w, h). Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Compute C(n,k) incrementally to avoid overflow
Width and height are counts, not indices
slides.narration: A single row or column has one path. Compute the binomial incrementally, multiplying then dividing, to keep values exact and avoid overflow.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Present DP first, then the formula
slides.narration: Present the DP first, then mention the formula. With obstacles, the formula breaks and DP is required.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Paths to a cell come from above or from the left; this is also a binomial coefficient.
slides.narration: To recap Number Of Ways To Traverse Graph: Paths to a cell come from above or from the left; this is also a binomial coefficient. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
